items.title: Why QXO sees homebuilders as its mainstay of future growth
items.description: QXO , which aims to have $50 billion in annual revenue within the next several years, is counting on homebuilders as a launchpad for growth. Chairman and CEO Brad Jacobs said Monday on a conference call that the company wants to supply builders with far more than lumber and trusses. QXO, which reports full Q3 2026 earnings after the market closes Thursday, has overhauled sales incentives, technology and pricing to become a primary supplier to production and custom builders. The push follows its acquisitions of TopBuild and Kodiak Building Partners this year and Beacon Roofing Supply in 2025. Collectively, these acquisitions gave QXO exposure to a wide range of building products, including residential and commercial insulation, roofing materials, waterproofing, lumber and building materials, siding and exteriors, drywall and interior finishes, installation services, and tools and equipment such as fasteners, compressors and safety gear. That broader footprint comes as the company’s core business is showing momentum. With $4.9 billion in combined revenue last quarter, the firm is well on its way to achieving Jacobs’ lofty annual revenue goal. QXO, which generates roughly 50% of its revenue from residential construction, reported preliminary Q3 2026 results earlier this week showing organic revenue per day improved for the second consecutive quarter. Companywide pricing rose 2.2% year over year, with nine of 11 business areas posting positive pricing, and daily sales were up 5.4% year over year by the end of October. Roofing and Waterproofing, QXO’s longest-held business after its April 2025 acquisition of Beacon Roofing Supply, grew daily sales 9.1%. Jacobs credited better on-time deliveries, invoice accuracy and inventory management for Beacon’s performance. Insulation was another strong performer, largely because of data center demand. Beyond those gains, Jacobs said during the conference call that homebuilders represent a big growth opportunity. He outlined how QXO plans to capture more of their business, along with several ways QXO plans to grow in 2027. Cross-selling to homebuilders offers room for growth During the call, Jacobs made it clear that QXO plans to cross-sell more to homebuilders, an important and growing customer segment. “Our strong relationships with production homebuilders are typically rooted in our truss and wall panel capabilities, as well as insulation, where we solve some of their greatest needs. At the same time, it creates an opportunity for us to expand share of wallet by becoming their primary supplier for a wider range of building materials, with the added value of scale to support their growth,” Jacobs explained. The company’s $17 billion acquisition of TopBuild , announced earlier this year, gave QXO an installation business with a presence at roughly 22,000 job sites every day. QXO, with an established distribution business, plans to leverage TopBuild’s installation services to supply more building materials, coordinate additional trades and manage more work and installations on individual job sites. QXO’s $2.25 billion acquisition of Kodiak Building Partners, announced in February, additionally gave the firm exposure to building materials like lumber, engineered wood, doors, windows, trusses and gypsum products. These materials are essential to the company’s plans to sell more to Kodiak’s many existing homebuilder customers. To incentivize cross-selling, Jacobs explained that QXO is changing its sales compensation structure to reward employees for selling customers a broader range of products across its businesses. Salespeople will have a financial incentive to introduce existing customers to other parts of QXO’s portfolio, including building materials and installation services. “Homebuilders are a big opportunity,” Jacobs said. “One of the main reasons we bought Kodiak is that they brought phenomenal relationships with the big production homebuilders and the custom builders. And they were mainly selling them lumber or trusses or engineered products. So, we’re building on those great relationships, and we’re going to sell them much more. We’ve already started talking to many of these customers about this. There’s a lot of appetite for this.” Five other margin and growth opportunities Cross-selling to homebuilders comprises just one focus area among QXO’s growth plans. Jacobs named five other areas where the company expects to improve margins and market share, including stronger supplier relationships, additional acquisitions, pricing improvements, smarter use of private-label products and technological improvements. Stronger procurement and supplier relationships As QXO continues to integrate and improve its Beacon, Kodiak and TopBuild acquisitions, the combined company intends to leverage its larger scale in negotiations with suppliers. The business has about $12 billion in combined spending, including about $11 billion in direct spending on products and materials. About $7.6 billion of that spending is with suppliers that serve at least two of QXO’s legacy businesses, including about $5 billion to suppliers serving all three. QXO plans to consolidate its supplier base to capture that overlap, which could allow the company to push for better pricing and rebates and standardize purchasing agreements across the businesses. “We want deep relationships with a smaller number of strategic supplier partners,” Jacobs said. “We want to be important partners with them and preferably their most important partner. And there’s quite a lot of overlap among the key suppliers across the three acquisitions we’ve recently done.” If QXO strengthens its supplier relationships, its homebuilder clients could see better product availability and service, making the company a more appealing primary supplier for builders, particularly as it expands its offerings through additional acquisitions. items.title: Reverse mortgage executives read the tea leaves to decipher the industry's next chapter
items.description: At this week's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Convention & Expo in San Antonio, executives offered their thoughts on the evolving product landscape and efforts to expand the sales force while cautioning that hurdles around consumer misperceptions remain. In a panel discussion held Tuesday and moderated by former NRMLA board member and current Texas Mortgage Bankers Association CEO Scott Norman , executives covered a wide range of topics including proprietary reverse mortgages , distribution efforts with traditional forward lenders and the potential for a broad marketing push to consumers. "I think one of the things that's held us back is our lack of distribution," said Jim Cory , managing director of Guild Mortgage 's reverse division. "It's such a sea change in our business to suddenly have to go from this beloved group that we have here and begin adding to it. And literally thousands of loan originators now have access to this product." Proprietary products push the envelope At a time when federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) have dropped to their lowest levels in about 10 years , private-label loans have stepped up to fill the void. Data compiled by New View Advisors showed that proprietary products accounted for 60% of all reverse mortgage volume in September 2026 — a share that is expected to continue growing. Melissa Macerato , the newly appointed president and chief commercial officer at Longbridge Financial , said that these products have changed business for the better and that the industry would "be in a very different place" without them. Longbridge has been among the lenders to introduce private-label solutions in recent years through its Platinum suite and HELOC for Seniors . Macerato said she expects to see more hybrid reverse mortgage products developed soon, with a focus on giving borrowers higher proceeds alongside mandatory but flexible payments. "In order to get that broader distribution, in order to have more exposure for our products, we're going to have to start speaking the language and developing products that more mainstream mortgage entities and loan officers really understand," she said. Jonathan Scarpati , chief production officer at Finance of America , told NRMLA attendees that the products "from 10 years ago are not reverse mortgages that everyone is selling today." His company has also been at the forefront of product innovation with its HomeSafe suite — including a second-lien option that allows borrowers to tap into their home equity without touching their low-rate first mortgage. But Scarpati believes that new products are meant to "cast a wider net" rather than replace the traditional HECM that's been the industry's cornerstone since the program was authorized in 1987. Mike Kent , senior vice president of corporate development and industry relations at Onity Mortgage , agreed. "The reason we have proprietary products is that [the HECM] set the baseline, it set the standards, it ushered in the appropriate regulation and safeguards for the product, and it kind of cleared the way for us to begin to innovate," Kent said. Scarpati also pushed back against the notion that more competition in reverse mortgages is a bad thing. "I think 2027 is a very pivotal moment for the industry in general," he said. "I think as the products continue to evolve, some of them are looking closer to the forward industry. … The closer we have our products look to what the forward industry is used to, the more growth and the more adoption we're going to get." Forward lenders could open their doors wider Cory said that lack of distribution has been a longstanding obstacle for the industry. But many of the large independent mortgage banks ( IMBs ) — including Guild, Rate , Fairway Home Mortgage and CrossCountry Mortgage — now have a visible presence in the space. According to Cory, the six largest IMBs have about 17,000 originators today, and business would expand significantly if this group alone put more resources into reverse. Jesse Allen , president of the 55+ lending division at Rate, said that while the largest IMBs have reverse mortgage options to offer borrowers, the ongoing hurdle is to get more engagement from loan officers. That work falls to reverse specialists, who must do a better job of sharing their knowledge and building relationships. "If you want other people to trust you, you have to really know your craft," Allen said. "Language matters. And so, as a reverse industry, I would encourage all of you to think about the language you use when you walk in with a traditional mortgage loan officer and a real estate agent. Use language that feels familiar to them and that will start to build trust." Some companies are introducing technology solutions to engage LOs who are unfamiliar with reverse products. Earlier this month, Nationwide Equities Corp. launched ReverseReach , a tool to help uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in existing customer databases and referral networks. And in July, Reverse Market Insight expanded its loan qualification tool to include Smartfi Home Loans ' proprietary products, part of Smartfi's push to get more traditional LOs involved. Scarpati said many lenders are looking for new opportunities as traditional purchase and refinance is expected to decline in 2027 . Home equity lending, including reverse mortgages, presents a massive opportunity as U.S. homeowners hold roughly $35 trillion in equity , including $15 trillion among those 62 and older. Lenders that don't diversify beyond traditional products may find tough sledding if liquidity issues and consolidation continue over the next 12 to 18 months, he added. items.title: A look at how apartment REITs did in Q3
items.description: A look at how apartment REITs did in Q3 Concessions continued to dampen earnings, but bright spots in San Francisco and New York City boosted a number of companies. Published Nov. 12, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print Add us on Google Getty Images In the fall of 2023, apartment REITs sounded the alarm during their earnings calls. The glut of apartment deliveries in many markets across the country was driving massive concessions from merchant developers. In turn, public apartment companies had to drop prices, even on older assets that normally don’t compete with new supply. Analysts ended up downgrading some of those companies. “This dynamic and its impact on our B-quality communities, in particular, was unexpected and unprecedented in my 30 years in the multifamily industry,” UDR CEO Tom Toomey said on the Highlands Ranch, Colorado-based REIT’s third-quarter 2023 conference call. Three years later, in Q3 2026, supply pressures are still popping up in unexpected ways, especially for Sun Belt-centric REITs. For instance, Camden Property Trust lowered its 2026 same-store revenue guidance. September performance, in particular, surprised the company and set the stage for that revision, according to CEO Alex Jessett. “It was a greater decline in traffic than we had expected,” he said. “And when we had the decline in traffic, obviously, you have to reduce your prices if you’re trying to increase traffic.” Despite continued issues with concessions, there were many bright spots in the REIT Q3 2026 earnings reports, including strength in San Francisco and New York City. items.title: The seasonal decline in housing inventory is in full force
items.description: Housing inventory Housing inventory has picked up recently, after mortgage rates went above 6.64% and then shot up toward 7.60%. Inventory growth had been very tame this year, with some weeks negative year over year. As housing inventory returns to normal levels, it takes weaker demand to get stronger growth and rates moving toward 7.60% did that. Still, it's more about sales taking longer to happen and demand being hit, because new listings data didn’t budge much recently. Now, we are in the full-blown seasonal decline as we get ready to prep for spring 2027. Inventory growth is running at 7.11% over last year even with easier comps, as last year demand was running toward a 9-month high in December of 2025. Weekly inventory change (Nov. 6-Nov. 13): Inventory fell from 902,740 to 895,988 Same week last year (Nov. 7-Nov. 14): Inventory fell from 842,257 to 836,487 New listings New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since 2022. One concern I had about higher rates is that more people might simply not list their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 due to higher rates. However, that hasn’t happened; we did see a more noticeable year-over-year decline this last week, but for the most part it’s been a healthy year. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 53,162 2025: 56,569 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point demand fell and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indices show growth between 1% and 2%. However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown. The price-cut percentage for last week: 2026: 43.% 2025: 42% 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market: we had hawkish Fed statements and hot inflation data. We were getting closer to mortgage rates below 7% for the holidays, but they made a big reversal from 7.17% to 7.50%. In addition, President Trump talked about raising tariffs against Mexico and we still have no deal with Iran. Pretty much everything you needed for rates to go lower went the other way — something I talked about in this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they did improve last week. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. However, we had a big reversal higher, and spreads improved some as the 10-year yield rose toward 5.14%. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads fell to 2.13% from 2.27% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 7.19% today, not 7.50% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.48% today, not 7.17% . Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last four weeks: housing demand has stabilized, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, higher rates most likely will impact this week’s data more than last week, but the last four weeks have shown if we can get rates back below 7% and just have them stick, we can work with this. Housing demand typically grows when rates get below 6.64% and fades when rates are above 7%, especially if the move in rates is fast, like we saw recently. Still, it was encouraging to see stabilization in the data when rates were trying to get below 7% again. Of course, we are seeing big year-over-year declines in this data line as rates were heading toward 6% last year. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 50,623 2025: 60,722 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We did have 8% week-to-week growth last week as rates tried to get below 7% the week before. I expect the next purchase application data to get hit as rates picked up. This data was very positive year over year when rates were under 6.64%, but not so much when it headed toward 7% and got to 7.60%. items.title: Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here's why
items.description: Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act 's institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels. According to the National Apartment Association ’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse , released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction , the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out. The industry's legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects. Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry. “I would say it hasn't normalized. In other words, it wasn't where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences , said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.” Uncertainty is still taking a toll Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position. “Capital's coming in, but it's not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it's really hard for them to write checks. According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere. “When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn't have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview. Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29. "Capital's just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market's still trying to find itself,” Tanner said. In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern. “Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned. The uncertainty surrounding Treasury’s proposed rulemaking The U.S. Department of the Treasury , which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, 'all right, built-to-rent is carved out.' But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said. Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy. Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued. The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects. Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban. items.title: Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls
items.description: America's apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding. National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11. The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%. The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables. Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month. Supply wave cools Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak. Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025. Landlords hit the brakes Improving rents haven't translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust , a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve's rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn. Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined. Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said. Camden's earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company's guidance midpoint. "A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment," Parsons wrote. Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters. Coasts and Midwest lead Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut. Sun Belt still lags Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%. San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%. Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%. items.title: Movement Mortgage seeks to recoup $1.2M from former LOs
items.description: Movement Mortgage wants two former loan officers to pay back a total of more than $1.2 million in signing bonuses after they left the company about a year into their three-year agreements. According to court and arbitration documents, Movement paid a total of $1,235,000 in “start-up payments” to loan officers Victor Shkolnikov and Igor Velyunskiy when they joined the company in March 2022. Shkolnikov received $835,000 and Velyunskiy received $400,000. The contracts said these payments were advances on future wages and had to be paid back in full if the loan officers left before working 36 consecutive months at the company. If they left early, the money was due within 30 days. Both Shkolnikov and Velyunskiy left Movement around March 2023, roughly one year into their three-year commitment. Public records show Shkolnikov now works as a loan originator with United Lending Team in Illinois, while Velyunskiy is with Smart Rate Lending LLC . Movement and the two former loan officers did not immediately respond to HousingWire ’s requests for comment. National Mortgage News first reported the dispute. Movement started arbitration in February 2024, and the cases were combined before arbitrator H. William Constangy. The LOs pushed back , filing counterclaims that accuse Movement of breach of contract, unjust enrichment, fraudulent inducement and violations of the Truth in Lending Act. In July, the arbitrator ruled in favor of Movement. The decision said the employment agreements were valid contracts and that the two breached the contracts when they did not repay the start-up payments after leaving before the 36-month mark. All of their counterclaims were dismissed. The award says the repayment amount will also accrue interest at North Carolina ’s legal rate of 8% per year, starting in April 2023, which the arbitrator treated as the date of the breach. The arbitrator did not order either side to pay the other’s legal fees, so each party must cover its own attorneys’ costs. In early November, Movement asked the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina, Charlotte Division , to confirm the arbitration award and turn it into a court judgment. That would make it easier for the lender to collect the money if it isn’t paid voluntarily. Related More: Lawsuit Loan Officer Movement Mortgage

items.title: Members Of Congress Have Questions For Brookfield After Its Mass Mobile Home Purchase
items.description: Brookfield quietly closed on the acquisition of the largest privately held manufactured housing portfolio in the United States this year, prompting some members of Congress to inquire about the investment giant’s plans for the properties it now owns. Bisnow/Ethan Rothstein Brookfield purchased Yes Communities from GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, in the second quarter, public filings and statements from Brookfield management indicate. Brookfield hasn’t publicized its acquisition of the Denver-based operator of nearly 300 manufactured home developments, but three Democrats from the House of Representatives nonetheless sent a letter to the firm last month voicing concern about the purchase and seeking pledges for tenant protections. Reps. Maxwell Alejandro Frost, Gabe Vasquez and Rashida Tlaib asked management at New York-based Brookfield Asset Management, the publicly traded arm of Toronto-based Brookfield, and Brookfield Real Estate Group to provide assurances that residents’ quality of life wouldn’t be impacted by the deal. The representatives gave BAM until Nov. 20 to respond. The asset management giant hadn’t yet replied as of mid-November, Frost’s office confirmed to Bisnow on Nov. 9. Brookfield didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment. It hasn’t formally announced the acquisition, which was first rumored to be in the works in September 2025, but BAM said in second-quarter filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it acquired “the largest privately held U.S. manufactured home portfolio.” Yes Communities operates more than 55,000 housing sites across the U.S., with a focus on the Southwest, Midwest and Southeast. A purchase price for the portfolio is unknown, but BAM said it spent $5.2B in the second quarter on its real estate business, including the manufactured home portfolio and the take-private of an industrial outdoor storage portfolio. Brookfield announced a $1.2B all-cash deal in February to buy Peakstone Realty Trust, a REIT with 60 IOS properties and 16 traditional industrial assets. In its second-quarter filings, Brookfield Real Estate Income Trust disclosed a new investment in a 2% ownership interest in 294 manufactured housing properties at a book value of $86.6M, which aligns with the number of properties under the Yes Communities banner. BAM Chief Financial Officer Hadley Peer Marshall also disclosed on the second-quarter earnings call that a Brookfield fund had made its first investment by deploying capital to Yes Communities. Other affiliates of Brookfield may have also contributed capital for the Yes Communities acquisition. Brookfield REIT said in an investor presentation on its website that as of Sept. 30, it owned a 294-community manufactured housing portfolio across 23 states, the same number of states Yes Communities is active in. Wikimedia Commons; Office of Maxwell Frost Democratic Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Gabriel Vasquez and Maxwell Frost have asked Brookfield about its acquisition of Yes Communities. Executives from Brookfield held one virtual meeting with residents and their advocates following the acquisition that was facilitated by the Private Equity Stakeholder Project and MHAction, two nonprofit advocacy groups, PESP confirmed to Bisnow . GIC and another unnamed institutional investor acquired a 71% equity interest in Yes Communities in 2016, with Stockbridge Capital Group holding on to the remaining stake. Brookfield was reportedly in talks with GIC about acquiring its stake for more than $10B, and it is unclear exactly the size of Brookfield's interest in Yes Communities or how much it paid. In their letter from Oct. 13, the three members of Congress sought details about the acquisition. The letter outlines previous tenants' complaints with Yes Communities for high rent increases, excessive fees and neglect of routine maintenance and says that Brookfield “has the opportunity to change this scenario” and “support meaningful protections for its residents.” “Given the challenges our constituents have experienced at Yes! properties, as well as broader concerns about the private equity business model, we seek assurances that Brookfield will prioritize improving residents’ quality of life and protecting their economic and housing stability, rather than exacerbating the economic challenges they already face,” the representatives wrote. The letter specifically asks Brookfield to disclose whether it plans to increase rents by more than 3% annually, to outline its policy regarding new and existing fees, and to confirm whether it will refrain from serial eviction filings for routine rent collection. The letter asks BAM to commit to meet regularly with tenants and to cooperate with tenant groups that are seeking to collectively purchase their communities. Corporate ownership of single-family properties has for a decade been an issue in some political corners, but it spilled into the mainstream in recent years, including with the debate around the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and the focus on affordability from candidates in midterm races across the country. The housing legislation that made it to the president’s desk includes new restrictions on existing home purchases from institutional investors but carves out broad exemptions for new development of single-family communities built as rentals. items.title: Get Out From Behind Your Desk: 5 Tips On Making Senior Management
items.description: Greystar Director Emily Papworth laid out the stark facts at Bisnow ’s Women Leading Real Estate event this month: 44% of those at middle management level in UK property are women, but that figure drops to just 26% when it comes to senior management. Jo McNamara taking the top spot at British Land is a positive example of a woman occupying one of the highest-profile jobs in UK property. But as a whole, the industry still lags when it comes to diversity. There is no silver bullet to change that, but the event featured a plethora of advice for those looking to progress their career to the top levels. Embrace Complexity And Find Your Niche Bisnow/Daniel Sikpi Mishcon de Reya's Anju Suneja and Mirastar's Ekaterina Avdonina Mirastar CEO Ekaterina Avdonina is a rare example of a female founder and CEO in property, having set up the specialist logistics investment and development platform in 2019, after founding Delin Properties in 2011. Avdonina said logistics, traditionally one of the most male property subsectors, appealed to the logical brain of someone who actually grew up in a family of rocket scientists. Logistics is a global business where occupiers consider specific location, transport, infrastructure links, labour, real estate and the long-term plans around the investments in those buildings. “That complexity really inspired me, and it was worth specialising,” she said. You Won't Succeed Sat At A Desk The work senior leaders do is different to that of middle management and the general workforce. A lot less of it is done from behind a computer. “The work is different, and that's probably been the biggest pivot for me over the last 18 months,” said Nisha Kerai, Legal & General head of operations and asset management for build-to-rent and purpose-built student accommodation. “When I go into the office, I make time to walk around and understand what's going on in the business, what will add value to the business, and thinking about new ideas, because it's not your job to do the ‘do’ anymore.” Advice Helps You Prepare, But Advocacy Helps You Progress Bisnow/Daniel Sikpi L&G's Nisha Kerai, Kennedy Wilson's Lottie Outen, Workman's Vicky Cotton, Ogier's Katharine Marshall and BDO's Rebecca Jones Before working for Kennedy Wilson , Lottie Outen, now managing director, advised the U.S. investor in her previous role as an investment banker at J.P. Morgan . Previous Kennedy Wilson Europe CEO Mary Ricks wanted to hire Outen and pushed for the appointment internally, giving her the opportunity to step up to what Outen described as the next level. “The difference here is that it wasn't just her advice that was beneficial — it was her willingness to put her credibility behind me and make that move happen,” Outen said. “Don't just try to recognise talent, but actually try to create opportunity for it.” Don't Presume Everyone's The Same How to bring people back into a company after a career break, be that maternity or care leave or a sabbatical, is one of the thorniest issues in the corporate world — it remains one of the key barriers for women attaining senior leadership positions, panellists said. Executive coaching provided by companies can be a big help for individuals, L&G’s Kerai said — there is no reason to presume people will be able to negotiate a period they have never experienced before. But there is also the need to appreciate there is no one-size-fits-all solution for a situation that affects everyone differently. “You want to be solutions-driven, so you're jumping to what you think you would want in their shoes. You're not in their shoes,” Ogier partner Katharine Marshall said. “So the most important thing, actually, is to listen to them.” Be Loud Loud people tend to get what they want in companies, Kerai said, so don’t be afraid to speak up. “I ask for a pay rise and a promotion every six months, full year, midyear, and people laugh when I say this,” she said. “But the worst that's going to happen is somebody says no, and then the second time they say no,” she added, pointing out that there has never been any negative impact on her career. “They might even say no four times, but they'll be embarrassed the fifth time. So you'll probably get what you want at that point.” Likewise, she said, there is value in getting loud for someone else, like directing the conversation back to someone being talked over in a meeting or advocating for someone who is being overlooked for promotion because they are not putting themselves forward. items.title: MAG Partners Taps Former Swire Exec For Miami Debut
items.description: After four years as senior vice president of development at Swire Properties , Kevin Davenport is joining MaryAnne Gilmartin 's team to lead her Manhattan-based firm's South Florida expansion. Courtesy of MAG Partners Kevin Davenport previously worked at Swire Properties and BGRE, formerly Brookfield Properties. MAG Partners named Davenport the senior vice president and head of development of South Florida, according to a release. The company is also looking to lease office space in Downtown Miami, reported Commercial Observer, which first reported the announcement . "Miami has grown into a global city, with the capital, talent and demand to support large, complex, mixed-use projects," MAG Partners wrote in a LinkedIn post on Thursday . "The projects that will define the region are being built now, and they depend on strong partnerships and teams that know how to deliver at scale. That is the work we do." The new role comes after MAG sought to hire a seasoned development executive to head a mixed-use tower with a hotel, luxury condos and retail spanning more than 1M SF at the beginning of this year. It is unclear where MAG is in the process of the unnamed project. MAG Partners declined to disclose any details about its Miami office lease and the project. Davenport's recent work with Swire included leading the development of the 2.7M SF Residences at Mandarin Oriental , Miami, which broke ground last month . He also led the predevelopment of Swire's planned 1.7M SF One Brickell City Centre office project before it was canceled and the site was sold to The Melo Group last year. Before Swire, Davenport spent 10 years at Brookfield Properties , which rebranded to BGRE in July, and held positions at Hines and the Blackstone Group , according to his LinkedIn. “MaryAnne and the MAG Partners team share my development ethos: a commitment to great design, thoughtful execution and creating places that have a lasting impact,” Davenport said in a statement. “I’m excited to build the company’s presence in South Florida.” This will be MAG Partners' first known venture into South Florida, according to its website. Gilmartin spearheaded the development of the Barclays Center basketball arena while working as an executive with Forest City Ratner before she was named CEO in 2013. After more than two decades with the company, she stepped down from her role and founded MAG Partners in 2018. MAG Partners has designed, built and operated more than 16M SF of office, residential and mixed-use projects with a total value of more than $10B, according to the release. The company has a handful of projects in New York, mainly mixed-income multifamily buildings, according to its website, and is now developing 122 Varick St. in Hudson Square with Global Holdings. New York-based companies have long had a presence in South Florida, but as the region grows in popularity, drawing the ultra-wealthy and their companies , more pros are dividing their time between the Big Apple and the Magic City. items.title: Could Budapest be the next digital nomad hotspot?
items.description: Why Hungary is a digital nomad hotspot Hungary ranked fifth for digital nomads on a 2025 list of countries, behind Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Montenegro and the Bahamas. The index, compiled by visa information website VisaGuide, considered factors such as taxes, income and cost of living. Vindisch, who has worked in many European and North American cities, but has Hungarian roots, said Budapest feels different. "I've been in locales that are super beautiful, well organized, great facilities, but they lacked a personality ... I've never been able to replicate the feeling that Budapest holds anywhere else," she said. EU citizens can work remotely from Hungary long-term if they meet certain requirements, while Hungary's White Card scheme, which provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU, requires a net monthly income of at least 3,000 euros ($3,370). Coworking space Liftoff in Budapest is located in a former elevator factory, where elevators for the Hungarian Parliament Building were made. Liftoff Coworking There are around 35 co-working spots in central Budapest, according to the Coworking Hungary Association, several of which are in the bustling District VI, near the fashionable bars and restaurants of the Jewish Quarter. Alongside these hubs, the city offers around 35 serviced offices, including locations from larger providers such as Regus and DBH Flex. "Budapest has its own vibe," said Áron Levendel, a founder of co-working space Kaptar, which is within view of the city's striking St Stephen's Basilica. "Whoever wants to connect, make friends or meet people, has an easy job. Whoever wants to have fun, learn or get experiences in English, will have the challenge of choosing from hundreds of options every evening," he said. 'Community' offices Levendel and his co-founders are organizational developers who wanted a workplace that was both sociable and professional. In 2010, they came up with the idea for Kaptar (the word means "hive" in Hungarian). "Gmail was already there, but most of the work was not in the cloud or online yet; people had folders and papers. Digital nomads were not a thing," Levendel told CNBC by email. "Co-working" also wasn't a term in common use at the time, so he called the space a "közösségi iroda," or community office. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Kaptar has grown more than 30% every year, according to Levendel, including a "wave" of digital nomads who joined after the pandemic, often arriving initially for a month but staying for up to a year. Overseas members either keep an existing job and work remotely, or they are freelancers who can travel, Levendel said. Coworking space Liftoff has an international community from central and eastern Europe as well as the U.S., the United Arab Emirates and Israel. Liftoff Coworking Mónika Gyurity opened co-working space Liftoff in 2019. After a career as a television executive, she wanted to expand her digital skills and bring different generations together to learn from each other. Located in a former elevator factory close to Budapest's central Nyugati station, Liftoff attracts a mix of professionals — including short-term visitors in need of a workspace, as well as remote employees working for international companies. One of Liftoff's team members is also a remote worker who regularly participates in Nomad Cruise voyages, or "workation" trips that combine a conference program with land excursions. Gyurity expects the digital nomad trend to continue, noting that AI now allows individuals to create and launch services or businesses without the resources of a large organization. "More people will be able to imagine their knowledge, skills and opportunities outside the traditional corporate world," she said. At the same time, she recommends that those in the corporate world spend time in a co-working environment. "Most people are there because they are trying to solve something," she said. "Every day I meet younger people who are at a very different stage of their lives and careers, use different tools, and approach problems differently. We can learn from each other." Co-working challenge A few streets north of the Hungarian Parliament building and steps from the River Danube sits Kubik, a co-working space where roughly 20% of members are digital nomads working in IT, software development, design or marketing. According to co-owner Éva Mocsár, many of these professionals split their time between Budapest and warmer climes, with some choosing to escape the Hungarian winter in Argentina, before returning in the spring. About 20% of Kubik's members are digital nomads, said co-owner Éva Mocsár. Kubik As with other co-working hubs, one of Mocsár's primary challenges is recruiting new members, particularly as larger office spaces compete with Kubik on price. "Co-working is closely connected to the office market, and Budapest has a huge amount of office space, a lot of it empty," she said. items.title: Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.
items.description: Hottest outdoor storage property markets The numbers help explain the appetite. Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses. Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically. The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial. Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025. Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn't missed the game. "We are still in the very early innings," Petrillo said. Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots. "It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added. Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors. "Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said. Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said. "Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added. Zoning is the biggest challenge. "If you don't understand the city's plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they're trying to phase out," Cheema said. CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community's plan for its future. Advantages over traditional industrial, multifamily real estate Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields. "Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said. For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. "We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space," Sutterer added. Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS. Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. But unlike the local businesses that tend to fill up shallow-bay sites, IOS tenants range from local businesses to those with investment-grade credit ratings, offering investors the potential for both yield and creditworthy tenants. And institutional money is making IOS more competitive. "Institutional capital has increased competition in IOS, and property values and lease rates have risen overall," Sutterer said. He added smaller investors can still find opportunities below institutional deal-size thresholds, although that does not mean every smaller deal is priced fairly. "We see opportunities to add value and earn yield in deals below $3 million–$5 million," Sutterer said. items.description: October 2026 Hottest Housing Markets By Hannah Jones Nov 13, 2026 Highlights Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, Conn. claimed the top spot in October for the first time since a summer run on top from May – July 2026. Buyer demand remains highly concentrated in the hottest markets, where listings attracted 2.6 times the national average number of views per property. The Midwest and Northeast were the only regions represented in the Top 20 for the 37th consecutive month. The list was evenly split this month, with 10 markets in the Midwest and 10 in the Northeast. Homes in the hottest markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on market of 37 days, more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm. Among large U.S. metros, Jacksonville, FL posted the biggest year-over-year improvement, jumping 70 spots to rank 189th nationally. The Hartford, CT metro moved up one spot from last month to claim the top spot on the hottest housing markets list for the first time since the summer. Hartford has ranked in the top 20 a total of 57 times, but has claimed the top spot only eight times. Located in New England, midway between Boston and New York, Hartford is an ideal landing spot for homebuyers looking to take advantage of the relatively low home prices in an otherwise pricey part of the country. In October, Hartford attracted 4.1 times the national average number of viewers per property. Homes sold in just 37 days, one day slower than a year ago but almost a month faster than the national norm. At a median listing price of $440,000, Hartford is priced just above the national norm, in a region generally priced well-above. Realtor.com’s Market Hotness rankings take into account two aspects of the housing market: 1) market demand, as measured by unique views per property on Realtor.com, and 2) the pace of the market as measured by the number of days a listing remains active on Realtor.com. That flexibility concentrates demand, and inventory in these markets remains well below pre-pandemic norms. The pull shows up in buyer traffic, with all six New England markets on the list drawing at least 2.6 times the national average views per property, at or above the Top 20 average. For shoppers, widening the search within the region means more options but not much relief from competition, since the affordability that draws buyers to one market is drawing them to its neighbors as well. The biggest movers were still fairly low on the overall list, ranging from 73rd for San Francisco to 216th for Denver. Four of the five biggest movers were located in the West, with three in California and one in the South. Though the South and West remain outside the nation's hottest markets, some areas are beginning to show growing demand and faster time-on-market. San Francisco stands out, with homes selling more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm, an acceleration likely boosted by the area’s ongoing AI boom . items.title: How Training Veterans in Skilled Trades Could Speed Up Homebuilding and Ease Housing Costs
items.description: A severe shortage of skilled workers entering the residential construction sector has had a major impact on affordability, but the Home Builders Institute (HBI) believes the country’s large veteran population may be part of the solution. The skilled labor shortage has led to an increase in construction time, with each home taking nearly two months longer to build, according to an HBI study . Due to the delays, there was a reduction of 19,000 homes built in 2024, representing an economic loss of over $8 billion, the study found. Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimated that the construction industry needs to attract roughly 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and 456,000 new workers in 2027 to meet demand for construction services. There are a number of factors in the past 30 years that have led to the labor shortage, according to HBI CEO Ed Brady . First, a strong push for four-year degrees led many young people toward academic careers rather than trades. With more people retiring from the workforce than entering, the shortage began. The issue was compounded during the financial crisis of 2008, when the residential construction field lost tons of skilled workers because there wasn’t enough work. Without enough housing construction, workers left for jobs in manufacturing and hospitality or retired early, according to Brady. More recently, rocky immigration policies have challenged the skilled labor workforce, Brady explains. When finding a solution to the shortage became dire, HBI believed that the veteran and transitioning military population was “an untapped market.” The result was the HBI Military Services Program, which trains veterans, transitioning military service members, and their dependents in skilled trades. On Monday, HBI and Invitation Homes announced a new partnership that will continue HBI’s mission to create opportunities for transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families. The partnership includes an unspecified investment from Invitation Homes in HBI’s Military Services Program. It will also open doors for former military service members who complete HBI training to access job opportunities with the premier leasing and management company. For nearly a decade, HBI has been raising awareness of the benefits of a career in a skilled trade among former members. It has proceeded to train, certify, and assist veterans and their families in finding successful careers. HBI’s Military Services Program was supported early on by major companies like The Home Depot Foundation and Dewalt. It was recently given a $1 million gift from Google.org , and now Invitation Homes has joined the worthy cause. These vital investments help HBI reach even more service members on their mission, according to Brady. “It provides scale. We’re not changing our model—we feel like our model works. We introduce them to the industry, we train them in the industry, we certify them, we connect them to the industry to get a job,” Brady tells Realtor.com® . “But the dollars from Invitation Homes, the dollars that Google have given us to apply into the veteran space just gives us more scale. We can provide better service, and we can grow our programs to serve more veterans, more transitioning military, even the spouses of veterans.” Loading... Associated Builders and Contractors estimated that the construction industry needs to attract roughly 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and 456,000 new workers in 2027 to meet demand for construction services. (Stock image) Bloomberg via Getty Images Expanding training programs for former military could make a huge difference in the skilled labor shortage being experienced by residential construction. “In many cases, the demographic of soldiers that want to be outside, want to work with their hands, and have that physicality, it’s natural for them to look at our industry,” says Brady. “They’ve got more discipline, they know how to create a task and how to do a job. They have a desire to be productive and build a career.” Brady has also observed that many veterans want to “control their own destiny” once they leave the military. The desire to not be dependent on anyone else or an organization makes them great candidates for entrepreneurship, business ownership, and contracting roles. A veteran’s point of view For Philip Shealy , HBI offered a path when he was unsure of next steps. After spending five years as an Army infantryman at Fort Drum in New York and Fort Stewart in Georgia , he had no clue what he wanted to do next, Shealy recalls. He decided to take advantage of the DoD SkillBridge to learn some skills before departing the service. “I saw the HBI program and thought, even if I don’t go into the skilled trades like that, that will be information I hold for the rest of my life. It’ll be great for owning a home or just knowing a thing here or there,” Shealy tells Realtor.com. “But the program does a pretty cool thing where they bring in recruiters from local companies. And they brought one in that sounded like something I wanted to do. So I applied with him and ended up getting the job.” Shealy now works for Ace Electric, an electrical contractor in southern Georgia, alongside several fellow veterans who went through the same HBI program. items.title: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
items.description: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of the Comptroller of the Currency National Credit Union Administration For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16. The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding. When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed. Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks. items.title: Why EAH Housing moved into Oregon to buy 1K affordable units
items.description: Why EAH Housing moved into Oregon to buy 1K affordable units The California-based developer acquired 19 properties from Catholic Charities of Oregon and opened a new affordable community in Sacramento. Published Nov. 13, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Good Shepherd Village in Happy Valley, Oregon. Permission granted by EAH Housing Properties: 19 Buyer: EAH Housing Seller: Catholic Charities of Oregon Property type: Affordable Units: More than 1,000 Location: Oregon EAH Housing has built a large presence in California and Hawaii with more than 25,000 affordable homes across 240 properties. Earlier this week, the San Rafael, California-based nonprofit owner, manager and developer expanded north by purchasing more than 1,000 affordable homes in the Portland area from Catholic Charities of Oregon, according to a press release. The 19 properties, which include a mix of family, senior and supportive housing communities, are located in the Portland metro area, including Eugene, Sandy and Happy Valley. The acquisition represents the latest in a series of large affordable transitions over the past couple of years. “We view this acquisition as the beginning of a broader presence in Oregon and will continue exploring opportunities to expand our affordable housing portfolio across the state,” Katherine Fleming, EAH’s chief portfolio officer, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. “We are focused on identifying mission-aligned opportunities that support the long-term preservation and availability of affordable housing in high-need areas.” Oregon expansion Catholic Charities of Oregon was seeking a mission-aligned nonprofit partner committed to the long-term preservation of affordable housing and approached EAH, according to Fleming. “The acquisition represents a natural extension of the organization’s mission into the Pacific Northwest, where EAH Housing sees significant opportunities to address growing affordable housing needs,” Fleming said. While the acquisition allows EAH to continue preserving affordable housing, Catholic Charities will continue to provide supportive services to residents, according to the release. Guardian Real Estate Services will stay on as manager following the sale. Purchase and sale agreements are now in place for the transaction, which EAH and Catholic Charities have been working on since January 2026, per the release. Financial closings and property transfers are expected to occur on a rolling basis until the second quarter of 2027. Fleming said EAH is “evaluating opportunities for improvement across the properties to ensure they continue to provide high-quality affordable housing for Oregon residents for years to come.” Catholic Charities remains involved CEO of Catholic Charities Kaleen Deatherage said transitioning the properties to EAH Housing allowed them “to remain in the hands of a nonprofit deeply committed to affordable housing.” “Catholic Charities got into affordable housing to serve people,” Deatherage said in the release. “That purpose has not changed. What has changed is our understanding of where we can make the greatest impact.” Catholic Charities was represented by Jackson Ross of Newmark's Affordable Housing Advisors team. In addition to the Oregon acquisition, EAH also opened On Broadway, a new 140-unit affordable mixed-use housing community in Sacramento, according to a Nov. 13 news release shared with Multifamily Dive. The property, which includes one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments across two five-story buildings, serves individuals and families earning between 30% and 60% of the area median income. Thirty-seven homes are permanent supportive housing for individuals and families experiencing or at risk of homelessness. Major affordable deals The EAH Oregon acquisition is only the latest large affordable housing transaction in recent years. In May, nonprofit multifamily affordable housing investment manager National Equity Fund completed a massive deal acquiring National Affordable Housing Trust’s properties and fund management portfolio. In all, NEF is gaining 165 properties, encompassing 15,000 affordable homes nationwide, across 29 funds from NAHT. In December 2025, New York City-headquartered affordable housing preservation company Hudson Valley Property Group acquired a 22-property portfolio comprising 4,768 units across the western United States from Spokane, Washington-based Inland Group. In November 2024, New York City- and Los Angeles-based Standard Communities acquired a 100% affordable housing portfolio of over 6,000 apartment homes in more than 60 communities in four states. With the purchase of the portfolio, valued at over $1 billion, Standard entered Arizona, Colorado and Texas and grew its California portfolio to nearly 11,000 apartments. In May 2023, Chicago-based Nuveen acquired a portfolio of more than 12,000 units concentrated in New York City from New York City-based Omni Holding Co. This portfolio included several large apartment properties in the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens, as well as buildings in Maryland, Massachusetts, Texas and other states. items.title: Zillow Rental Market Report: Demand for Single-Family Rentals Surges – RISmedia
items.description: Report: Demand Surges for Single-Family Rentals Single-family rental demand is rising nationwide, with demand up 24.3% year over year as the cost of homeownership continues to outpace renting. Home Agents November 12, 2026, 3 pm Reading Time: 3 mins read Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. “For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.” The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). For more information, visit www.zillow.com . items.title: U.S. Treasury’s Proposed Regulations Concerning Title X Of The 21st Century ROAD To Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know – National Law Review
items.description: John Cagigas Email 678-390-3055 Bio and Articles Find Your Next Job ! Commercial Litigation Attorney Paralegal - Washington, Dist. Columbia Senior Attorney - Arizona or New Mexico Explore More Job Openings U.S. Treasury’s Proposed Regulations Concerning Title X Of The 21st Century ROAD To Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know by: John Cagigas , Winstead - News Alert Monday, November 9, 2026 Related Practices & Jurisdictions Real Estate Financial Institutions Banking Administrative Regulatory All Federal Print Mail Download />i Introduction On July 11, 2026, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 19521 (the “ Act ”). As discussed in our June 24 article, “Title X of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know” (the “ Initial Article ”), Title X of the Act generally bars a “ large institutional investor ” from buying—or entering into a contract to buy—a “ single-family home ” unless a statutory exception applies. Under the Act, a covered investor must be a qualifying for-profit entity engaged in the single-family rental (“ SFR ”) business that, alone or with others acting “ in concert ,” has direct or indirect “ investment control ” over at least 350 single-family homes. Homes acquired through statutory exceptions after July 11, 2026, are excluded from that count. For this purpose, a “ single-family home ” generally means a structure with no more than two dwelling units, excluding manufactured homes. On October 23, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury (the “ Treasury ”) issued proposed regulations under Title X (proposed 31 C.F.R. Part 36, the “ Proposed Regulations ”). The Proposed Regulations explain several exceptions for build-to-rent (“ BTR ”), renovate-to-rent, homeownership programs, creditor enforcement and institutional resales, as well as rules affecting investment funds and managers. However, some of the Treasury’s proposals could also complicate common BTR development and sale structures. As of the date hereof, the Proposed Regulations are not binding or final, and the Treasury expects additional rulemakings. Public comments on the Proposed Regulations will be due by November 23, 2026, and the statutory purchase prohibition under the Act becomes effective January 7, 2027, independent of when final regulations are adopted. Key Takeaways The headline for BTR is mixed: the Treasury proposes a purchase deadline of 18 months after a home receives its certificate of occupancy, but also confirms that qualifying homes can be resold repeatedly between covered institutional investors. The Treasury also proposes a written-program requirement for several exceptions and a more detailed test for passive investors. Important gaps remain that are unresolved in the Proposed Regulations, including how the Act applies to fund aggregation, equity transfers, pre-effective-date purchase contracts and BTR homes leased before an institutional sale. The discussion below distinguishes what Congress expressly provided in the Act from the additional conditions the Treasury now offers in the in the Proposed Regulations. BTR Protection: Greater Certainty, but a Narrower Initial Acquisition Window The Act expressly allows purchases under a BTR program in which a large institutional investor “ purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains ” newly constructed homes to be managed as rentals. Our Initial Article explained why that language appeared to protect traditional BTR development and institutional takeout sales. The Treasury’s proposed definition, however, focuses on when a home is purchased and how it is first occupied. Proposed § 36.5 would require a home acquired under the BTR exception to (i) have no previous owner-occupant, (ii) be purchased within 18 months after its certificate of occupancy (or local equivalent), and (iii) be first occupied by renters after the purchase. The Treasury rejected an alternative that would treat an older home as “ newly constructed ” solely because it was originally built and continuously used as a rental. The proposal does not separately explain how these purchase-focused requirements apply when an institutional investor itself constructs and retains the homes, a scenario the Act expressly includes. This may matter for merchant-builders that deliver a community in phases, lease homes as they are completed and sell the stabilized project in one transaction. Because the proposed deadline is tied to each home’s certificate of occupancy, earlier phases could fall outside the proposed BTR exception even while later phases qualify. The Treasury has not proposed a project-wide extension measured from the final phase or stabilization. Another statutory exception may be needed for homes that miss the 18-month window. A second issue concerns lease-up before closing. The proposed § 36.5(c) states that homes must be “ after the purchase, first occupied by renters .” That language appears to require that first-time rental occupancy occur after the institutional buyer purchases the homes, so a home already renter-occupied before sale would appear ineligible for this exception. The Proposed Regulations do not expressly disqualify pre-leased homes or analyze pre-sale lease-up, so clarification remains warranted before buyers rely on this exception. The Act permits BTR homes in both entirely rental and mixed rental/owner-occupied communities, and the Treasury confirms that the exception is not lost simply because a development also contains other property types. The rule still applies home-by-home: conventional apartment buildings with three or more dwelling units per structure generally fall outside the Act’s definition of “ single-family home ,” while qualifying SFR homes within the same development remain subject to the applicable exception.
